section.title: The Six Seals
section.sectionRationale: Having established in chapter 5 that the Lamb alone is worthy to open the scroll, John now shows the Lamb actually breaking its seals one by one. The first four seals form a tight unit of four horsemen, the fifth and sixth are each longer and distinct, and the seventh seal is deliberately delayed until 8:1, with chapter 7 forming an interlude between the sixth and seventh. This chapter is therefore its own coherent movement, the unleashing of six seals, ending on the terrified cry 'who is able to withstand it,' a question chapter 7 will answer.
section.thesis: As the Lamb breaks seal after seal, conquest, war, famine, and death ride out under God's sovereign permission, martyred souls cry out for justice from under the altar, and the created order itself convulses, so that every earthly power is left with nowhere to hide from the wrath of the One on the throne and of the Lamb.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the first seal, a rider bent on conquest; the second, third, and fourth seals, war, scarcity, and death riding together; the fifth seal, the martyrs' cry from under the altar; and the sixth seal, cosmic upheaval and universal terror before the wrath of the Lamb.

verses.text: Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say in a thunderous voice, “Come!”
So I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to {{nikao|overcome}} and conquer.

units.label: The second, third, and fourth seals

verses.text: And when the Lamb opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”
Then another horse went forth. It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword.
And when the Lamb opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” Then I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales.

And I heard what sounded like a voice from among the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a {{denarion|denarius}}, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine.”
And when the Lamb opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”

Then I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.
And when the Lamb opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the {{psyche|souls}} of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld.
And they cried out in a loud voice, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?”
Then each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer, until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed.
And when I saw the Lamb open the sixth seal, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red,
and the stars of the sky fell to the earth like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind.
The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.
Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free man hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.
And they said to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the {{orge|wrath}} of the Lamb.
For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?”

nikao.gloss: To conquer, to overcome, to be victorious. The first rider goes out already 'overcoming' and 'to conquer,' a doubled use of the same root that stresses relentless, ongoing military triumph. Revelation elsewhere reserves this verb for Christ and the overcoming saints, making its use here for a rider of judgment a deliberately unsettling irony.

denarion.gloss: A denarius, a Roman silver coin equal to a laborer's typical day's wage. That a whole day's pay would buy only a single day's ration of wheat, or barely three days of barley, pictures severe famine-level inflation, while oil and wine, the crop of deep-rooted trees and vines, are spared, showing scarcity held within limits God still sets.

psyche.gloss: Soul, life, the seat of a person's being. The souls under the altar are the martyrs whose lifeblood, poured out for their faithfulness, is pictured as a sacrifice at the base of the heavenly altar. They are consciously alive in God's presence, awaiting the completion of their number and the vindication their cry asks for.

orge.gloss: Wrath, settled and just anger, distinct from a sudden fit of rage. Here it is startlingly called the wrath 'of the Lamb,' fusing the image of gentle sacrifice with righteous judgment; the same Lamb who was slain for sinners is also the one whose wrath the unrepentant cannot stand before.

basic.context: The Lamb begins breaking the scroll's seven seals, and each breaking releases a vision. Four horsemen ride out in quick succession: conquest, war, scarcity, and death. Then the scene shifts to heaven, where martyred believers cry from under an altar, asking how long until God judges their killers; they are told to wait a little longer. Finally the sixth seal brings a cosmic shaking, sun and moon darkened, stars falling, mountains moved, and every class of person on earth, from kings to slaves, hiding in terror from the wrath of the One on the throne and of the Lamb.
basic.hermeneutics: Readers have long debated whether these seals describe events already fulfilled in the first century, patterns recurring throughout church history, a specific future tribulation, or timeless symbols of the kind of upheaval that marks every age until Christ returns. Wise interpreters hold these views with humility, since faithful readers disagree, but every view agrees on the chapter's central claim: history's calamities unfold only because the Lamb permits them, and God's people are never abandoned in the midst of them.
basic.originalLanguages: The first rider goes out nikao, conquering and to conquer, doubling the verb of victory that Revelation elsewhere reserves for Christ and His people, an unsettling echo. The third seal's denarion, a day's wage, buys barely a day's food, picturing severe scarcity. The martyrs are psyche, souls, consciously alive under the altar, crying for justice. And the terrified world hides from the orge, wrath, of the Lamb, the same Lamb once slain now revealed as the one whose judgment cannot be escaped.
basic.typology: The four horsemen echo the ancient covenant curses of sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts named in Israel's law. The martyrs' cry from under the altar recalls Abel's blood crying out from the ground in Genesis. And the cosmic darkening of sun, moon, and stars fulfills prophetic pictures of the Day of the LORD found throughout the Old Testament prophets, now applied to the climactic day of the Lamb's wrath.
basic.christ: It is the Lamb, and only the Lamb, who breaks each seal; every horseman rides, every martyr's cry is heard, and every cosmic convulsion happens strictly because He permits it. The chapter that began with His worthiness in chapter 5 continues here with His sovereignty over history's darkest hours, and it ends with the world recognizing, in terror rather than faith, that even the wrath they face is His.
basic.god: God governs even the world's worst violence and disorder; nothing here is outside His control, since it is the Lamb who authorizes each seal's release. Yet God is not indifferent to the suffering of His people; He hears the martyrs' cry and answers it, not by ignoring justice but by setting His own perfect timing for it, asking them to wait until the full number of the faithful has been gathered.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 1 and 6 describe four colored horses sent to patrol and report on the earth, an image John reshapes here as active agents of judgment. Ezekiel 14:21 names sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague together as God's four sore judgments. Joel 2:31 and other prophets describe the sun darkened and moon turned to blood before the great Day of the LORD, language this chapter directly echoes.
basic.oneStory: From Eden onward the Bible has warned that a world in rebellion against God will reap conquest, war, scarcity, and death, yet has also promised that God hears the cry of His suffering people. Here that whole story converges: the Lamb who was slain now sovereignly permits the very calamities the prophets foretold, martyrs are comforted rather than ignored, and even the mightiest of the earth are brought low before the wrath of the Lamb, driving every reader to ask which side of that day they stand on.

context.literary:
Chapter 6 is the first stretch of the scroll's contents, and it is built like a staircase with a landing. The first four seals share one pattern: the Lamb opens the seal, one of the four living creatures calls out 'Come!', and a horse of a different colour goes out. That fourfold set is the only place in the whole book where the pattern is this rigid. The fifth and sixth seals break it. Their scenes are longer, they are set in heaven and in the cosmos rather than on the road, and instead of a creature's command we hear human voices, first the martyrs and then the terrified kings.

Look at who speaks. Each of the first four calls comes from a creature before the throne, so the horsemen go out on an errand that begins at the throne. The riders are never described as acting on their own initiative. The second rider 'was granted permission', verse 4, and the fourth was 'given authority over a fourth of the earth', verse 8. John uses the passive voice again and again, the grammar of permission. The one who holds the keys is the Lamb of chapter 5, and nothing moves until He breaks a seal.

There is also a built-in progression of audiences. The horsemen ride across the earth, the martyrs speak from under the altar, and the sixth seal reaches the sky itself, so that the reader is carried from the road, to the sanctuary, to the heavens. The list of fleeing people in verse 15 has seven groups, kings to slaves, and the sevenfold list is the narrator's way of saying that no one is left out.

The chapter ends with a question and no answer: 'who is able to withstand it?', verse 17. The reader is meant to feel the weight of that question for a full chapter, because chapter 7 begins with 'After this' and supplies the reply.
context.historical:
The four colours and the four riders would have rung a bell for any hearer who knew the Prophets. In Zechariah's night visions horses of several colours patrol the earth for the LORD, Zechariah 1:8, and in Zechariah 6:1 to 8 chariots with coloured horses go out from before the Lord of all the earth. John reworks that scene, so that the patrolling horses become agents of judgment set loose by the Lamb. The other prophetic background is the list of 'four dire judgments' in Ezekiel 14:21: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. Verse 8 uses that same fourfold list almost word for word, and Leviticus 26:21 to 26 had earlier threatened the same disasters for covenant breaking.

The first hearers also lived with these things. Roman power was won by the sword and kept by it, so the 'peace' the empire advertised rested on conquest. The Parthians on the eastern frontier were famous mounted archers, and a rider with a bow was a figure of dread. Grain shortages were a recurring fact of city life in the Roman world, and the scale in verse 6 shows ordinary wheat selling at many times its normal price while the oil and wine, the luxuries of the better off, are left untouched, a quiet comment on whose pockets feel famine first. Plagues, too, ran through crowded cities.

Persecution is the fifth seal's setting. John writes from Patmos 'because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus', Revelation 1:9, and Antipas of Pergamum had already died, Revelation 2:13. The altar under which the martyrs lie also has a background in the Law, where the blood of sacrificed animals was poured out at the base of the altar, Exodus 29:12 and Leviticus 4:7. The sixth seal's language of earthquake, darkened sun and falling stars belongs to the Old Testament's stock of day of the LORD imagery, which the first hearers would have known by heart.
context.canonical:
The chapter is stitched from the Old Testament, and the New Testament speaks to it in turn. The horsemen draw on Zechariah 1 and 6, and the fourfold judgment draws on Ezekiel 14:21. The fifth seal's cry echoes the prayer of the exiles, 'How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy', Zechariah 1:12, and the Psalms that ask how long the wicked will triumph, Psalm 79:5 and Psalm 94:3. The voice of the slain is the voice of Abel's blood, which cried from the ground, Genesis 4:10. The sixth seal collects day of the LORD pictures from Joel 2:10 and 2:31, Isaiah 13:10 and Isaiah 34:4, and the hiding of the great ones is a reworking of Hosea 10:8, a verse Jesus has already quoted on the road to the cross, Luke 23:30.

The same sequence of war, famine and earthquakes appears in the Olivet Discourse, where Jesus calls these things 'the beginning of birth pains', Matthew 24:6 to 8. Revelation is not inventing a new scheme but giving a vision of what Jesus had told His disciples to expect between His departure and His return. Paul can say that neither famine nor sword will separate believers from the love of Christ, Romans 8:35 to 37, which is the same list of woes from the point of view of the people who suffer them.

Looking forward, the martyrs of the fifth seal are the first of several appearances of the slain, Revelation 12:11, Revelation 14:13 and Revelation 20:4. The rider named Death meets his end when 'Death and Hades' are thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:14. And the question that closes the chapter is the same one Malachi asks of the day of the LORD, 'who can endure the day of His coming?', Malachi 3:2, and Joel 2:11. Chapter 7 gives the answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John writes to churches who were tempted to read their suffering as proof that God had lost control, or that Rome had won. The chapter is meant to reverse that reading. The things that frighten them, the sword, hunger, the grave, the courts that kill believers, and even the sky coming apart, are all shown to be under the Lamb's hand. Nothing happens without 'Come!', and the riders are only 'given' what they do.

John also means the hearers to carry a particular habit into their own day: when a believer is killed for the faith, heaven is not silent. The martyr is not forgotten but is placed under the altar, given a white robe, and heard. The cry of verse 10 is allowed to stand in the Bible, and the answer, 'rest a little while longer', is meant to teach patience without teaching that the cry is wrong.

And he means the churches to feel the sober weight of the sixth seal, because the reason the world's powerful people run is that they finally see whose face and whose wrath they have been resisting. The wrath is the Lamb's own, which makes the picture of Christ in chapter 5 inseparable from the picture of Christ here. His gentleness and His judgment are the same Lamb. A hearer who has been told, in chapter 5, to weep no more because the Lion has conquered, is shown here what that conquest means for His enemies.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in this chapter is a command to the reader. It describes what the Lamb unleashes and what heaven says about it, and it is not an instruction to cause or celebrate any of it. Nobody is told to go to war, hoard grain or hasten the end. The one speech by humans that the chapter records, the martyrs' cry for vengeance, is reported without comment, and it should not be turned into a licence for believers to take vengeance themselves. In the Bible the right to avenge belongs to God, and the martyrs hand the matter back to Him by asking Him to do it.

What does carry across to the reader is the pattern of response. Believers may bring their anger at injustice to God in the form of a plain prayer, 'how long?', as the psalmists did. They are to accept that God's timetable for justice may be longer than they want, and they are to hold the hardship of the age as something the Lamb is Lord over rather than something that proves He is absent. A reader should not use the seals to build a timetable of current events. The chapter is about who is in charge, and a precise calendar is not what it was written to supply.

debates.question: Who is the rider on the white horse?

views.label: Christ, or the gospel He sends
views.case: Revelation 19:11 pictures Christ on a white horse with a name, Faithful and True, and white is the colour of victory and purity throughout the book. The crown and the going out to conquer fit a triumphant figure, and Jesus said the gospel must be preached to all nations before the end, Matthew 24:14. Some early readers took the rider as the spread of the gospel.

views.label: A conquering power opposed to Christ, or the spirit of conquest
views.case: The rider is one of four that come in a set, and the other three are plainly bringers of disaster. The bow is not Christ's weapon in 19:11, where the sword comes from His mouth. The rider is only 'given' a crown, and the first rider is introduced by the same call as the other three. Many take him as military conquest, with the Parthian archers as a background, and the seal as the first of the woes Jesus foretold.

debates.bearing: The reading that sees all four as judgments fits the set pattern, the lack of any Christ name here, and the Olivet parallel in which conquest comes with wars. The reading that sees Christ has real weight from the colour and from the unique word for the crown. In either case the chapter's main claim stands: the Lamb is the one who lets history move, and a reader need not settle the identity to take the point.

debates.question: Is the fifth seal about a fixed number or an open count?

views.label: A fixed number to be filled
views.case: The martyrs are told to wait 'until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed', verse 11. The verb of fullness suggests a total that God has already set. Many take this as a hint that God has a plan for the church's suffering and is not caught off guard.

views.label: A fullness without a counted total
views.case: The Bible elsewhere speaks of fullness without giving a figure, such as 'the full number of the Gentiles' in Romans 11:25. On this reading the verse means that persecution will keep coming until a complete company has borne witness, and John gives no number that the reader could work out.

debates.bearing: Either way the verse says that the suffering of believers has an end that God knows. The reader is not told how many, and should not try to work it out. What matters is that the martyrs are cared for in the waiting, with a robe and a place at the altar.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 says the first rider received a 'crown'. The Greek word is stephanos, the wreath of a victor or a person honoured, and not the diadema of a ruling king, which John uses for the dragon and the beast in Revelation 12:3 and Revelation 13:1 and for Christ in Revelation 19:12. It is worth noticing that John reserves the word for kingly crowns for those three figures and uses the athlete's wreath for the horseman, and the same word stephanos goes to the faithful in Revelation 2:10. A reader should not build too much on this, because John uses stephanos of the elders' crowns and the son of man's golden crown too, but it shows that the word alone does not decide who the rider is.

The riders are 'given' things again and again. Verse 2 has a crown given, verse 4 has a great sword given and permission granted, verse 8 has authority given. The verb is edothe, the passive of didomi, 'give'. It is commonly called the divine passive, since the unnamed giver is the one on the throne. The effect is to make each horseman a creature under authority, and the verb is repeated later of the beast, Revelation 13:5 and 13:7, so that the book's enemies are always on a lead.

In verse 6 the 'quart' is the choinix, roughly a day's ration of grain for one man, and the denarius was a labourer's daily wage. Wheat at that price means a worker's whole pay buys only enough for himself, with nothing left for a family. The barley is cheaper, three portions for the same coin, the food of the poor, and the command 'do not harm the oil and wine' is a limit placed on the famine.

Verse 8 calls the fourth horse chloros, from which we get 'chlorophyll'. It means the green of fresh growth, but also the sickly pale of a corpse, and the English 'pale green' catches both. The rider is named Death, and Hades 'followed close behind', so that the grave is shown in the train of the one who fills it.

The martyrs are the 'slain', verse 9. John uses sphazo, the same verb he used of the Lamb who appeared to have been 'slain' in Revelation 5:6, so the language ties the servants' death to their Master's. The cry of verse 10 addresses God as despotes, 'Lord' in the sense of absolute master, a word that occurs only here in Revelation and is chosen for a prayer of dependence. They ask Him to 'avenge', from the verb ekdikeo, which means to give justice and to bring right to the wronged, as the cry of the oppressed widow in Luke 18:3 uses a related word.

The question in verse 17 asks 'who is able to withstand it?', in Greek tis dynatai stathenai, literally 'who is able to be made to stand'. The verb is the same as the multitude's standing in Revelation 7:9, where the perfect participle hestotes shows that they are standing already. The two verses are joined at the level of the vocabulary, and the answer is in the word.

typology.type: The altar where the blood was poured out, Exodus 29:12
typology.fulfillment: At the base of Israel's altar the blood of the sacrifice was poured out, and Leviticus 17:11 says the life is in the blood. John sees the martyrs' lives, their blood, as being under the altar, so that their death is understood in the language of sacrifice. The correspondence is real but not exact, since the martyrs do not atone for anyone. The escalation is in Christ, whose blood really does cleanse, Hebrews 9:13 and 14, and by whose blood the multitude of chapter 7 washes its robes. Paul can speak of being poured out as a drink offering, Philippians 2:17 and 2 Timothy 4:6, but only Christ's blood, once for all, takes away sin.

The four disasters named by Ezekiel were the covenant curses that fell on Jerusalem when it broke faith, and each had been foretold in Leviticus 26. John pictures them riding out again, now on a larger stage. The correspondence is the pattern of sword, famine, plague and wild beasts, and verse 8 takes the Ezekiel list almost unchanged. The escalation is that in Revelation the judgment is released by the Lamb rather than by a covenant lawsuit against one city, and it reaches 'a fourth of the earth'. The type falls short in one respect: the limits placed on the riders, a fourth and no more, show that these are warnings, and not yet the final reckoning.

typology.type: The 'how long' of the suffering righteous, Zechariah 1:12
typology.fulfillment: The angel of the LORD asked how long God would withhold mercy from Jerusalem, and received a comforting word. The martyrs of the fifth seal ask the same question, and receive a white robe and a short wait. The pattern is that the cry of God's people is heard in heaven and answered in His time. The escalation is that the cry now rises from those who have died for Christ, and is answered by Christ's own work, who sits at the right hand and makes intercession, Romans 8:34. The type falls short because Zechariah's answer was about a city, while the martyrs' answer concerns the end of the age.

typology.type: The shaking of the heavens, Isaiah 34:4 and Haggai 2:6
typology.fulfillment: The prophets describe the sky rolled up and the stars falling as the day when God shakes the order of creation. Isaiah 34:4 gives the rolled scroll and the figs falling from the tree, and Haggai 2:6 speaks of God shaking heaven and earth once more. The author of Hebrews takes up Haggai to say that the removal of what can be shaken leaves the unshakable kingdom, Hebrews 12:26 to 28. The correspondence is the shaking that exposes false security. The escalation is that those who belong to Christ receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken, so that for them the end of the old order is not a loss. The type does not say who will stand, and the next chapter answers that.

study.christ:
The chapter will not let us pull apart the Lamb of chapter 5 and the judge of chapter 6. The one who is called the Lion and who appears as a slain Lamb, Revelation 5:5 and 5:6, is the same one whose wrath makes kings run for the caves. John does not apologise for the combination. The title 'the wrath of the Lamb' is deliberately paradoxical, since a lamb is the least threatening animal on the farm. It means that the wrath of God comes through the sacrificed one, and that the people who have refused His sacrifice have nowhere else to go. The gentleness of the cross and the terror of the day of judgment come from the same person, which is why Jesus, on His way to the cross, could quote the cry of the hiding crowds as a warning for the day to come, Luke 23:30.

The chapter leads to Christ by the keys He holds. In Revelation 1:18 He says He holds the keys of Death and of Hades, and here Death and Hades ride, but only as far as they are 'given'. The fourth rider has a name and a limit, and the Lord of both is the one who died and lived. What looks like death's reign over a quarter of the earth is a dependent authority on loan.

It also leads to Christ by solidarity with the martyrs. They are 'slain', the same word that was used of Him, and they are slain for the word of God and the testimony they held. In dying they are following the pattern of the Lamb, who conquered by being slain, Revelation 12:11. Their white robes anticipate the robes of the multitude who washed them in the Lamb's blood, and their appearance under the altar says that what is done to His people is done in His shadow. Jesus told Saul on the road to Damascus, 'Why do you persecute Me?', Acts 9:4, so the cry of the martyrs is, in a sense, also a cry about Him.

Finally, the chapter leads to Christ in what it leaves unsaid. 'Who is able to withstand it?' has one answer in the New Testament: the one who stood when everyone else fell. Jesus stood before Pilate and the cross and the grave, and He stands as the High Priest of His people. Those who are 'in Him', Romans 8:1, are not condemned, and they are not left to run for the rocks. The proper response to verse 17 is not despair but running to the Lamb instead of from Him, as the multitude of chapter 7 does.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows is that God is sovereign over evil without being its author. Every horseman is a creature who is 'given', and there is a clear difference between permitting a judgment and performing a sin. The sword that takes peace from the earth is wielded by men who slay one another, and yet verse 4 says the rider was granted the permission. Scripture holds both truths together, as it does for Joseph's brothers, Genesis 50:20, and for the cross, Acts 2:23. This is not a safe or tidy doctrine, but it is the only one that lets the believer pray in a violent world, since a God who did not hold the reins could not answer anything.

Second, God is holy and true, which the martyrs say in the same breath as they ask for justice: 'O Lord, holy and true', verse 10. They do not doubt His character even while they question His timing. Their cry rests on His holiness, because a holy God cannot be indifferent to blood, and on His truth, because He has promised to judge. The Bible's God is not offended by the question 'how long?', and He gives the martyrs an answer of tenderness, a robe, and a call to rest.

Third, He is patient. The 'little while longer' is a reminder that the delay in justice is not a lapse. Peter says the Lord is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish, 2 Peter 3:9. The same patience that frustrates the martyrs is the mercy that keeps the door of repentance open for their killers. The chapter holds that tension honestly, without claiming it can be dissolved.

Fourth, God is a God of wrath, and the chapter does not blur it. The sixth seal shows what wrath does to the confidence of kings and the rich, and the people hiding in the rocks have no sense that they have been treated unfairly. They know whose face it is. A doctrine of God that keeps only the mercy would miss the whole of verses 15 to 17.

For worship this means two things at once. We can praise the One who holds the keys when the news is dark, and we can also fear Him in the right way, with the reverent awe that belongs to the Lord whose wrath is the other side of His love for the slain. Both responses are in the book, and the next chapter will turn the fear into singing.

crossReferences.note: The riders on horses of different colours who patrol the earth for the LORD, and the angel's 'how long' prayer, are the seed of this whole chapter. John takes Zechariah's scouts and the exiles' cry and makes them agents of judgment and the cry of the martyrs.

Chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses go out from before the Lord of all the earth, and they are called the four spirits of heaven. The mission from the throne to the four quarters is the pattern behind the four horsemen who ride out when the Lamb opens each seal.

The Lord names four dire judgments, sword, famine, wild beasts and plague, as the penalty for faithlessness. Revelation 6:8 reuses exactly this list for the fourth rider, so the seals read as covenant judgments rather than random catastrophe.

The covenant curses include the sword that avenges the covenant, plague, and a famine in which ten women bake their bread in one oven and the people eat without being satisfied. Verse 6 of our chapter, with its measured grain, matches this picture of scarcity sharply.

Jesus tells His disciples to expect wars, famines and earthquakes, and calls them the beginning of birth pains. The seals show the same list from heaven's side, and the Lord's warning is that these things are not the end itself, so the disciples should not be alarmed.

Abel's blood cries out from the ground, and the LORD hears it. The martyrs under the altar are the later voices of that same blood, and the note that God hears the cry of the slain runs all the way from the first murder to the fifth seal.

Isaiah foresees the stars dissolving and the skies rolled up like a scroll, and the stars falling like figs from the fig tree. John uses the very images in verses 13 and 14, which shows that the sixth seal is described in the language of the prophets' day of the LORD.

The people will say to the mountains 'Cover us!' and to the hills 'Fall on us!' when their idolatry is judged. Verse 16 repeats the cry, and Jesus quoted it on the way to Calvary, Luke 23:30, which links the fall of a city and the end of the age.

The prophet asks who can endure the day of the Lord's coming and who can stand when He appears. The question that closes Revelation 6 is the same one, and the answer is a refiner's fire for the washed and a terror for the proud.

The very next scene answers verse 17. Those who stand before the throne in white robes are the ones who washed their robes in the Lamb's blood, and the word 'stand' is the same word as the end of chapter 6. The seal on their foreheads holds back the harm.

John again sees the souls of those beheaded for the word of God and their testimony, and this time they live and reign with Christ. The fifth seal's waiting martyrs reach their reward here, and the robe given in 6:11 is the pledge of it.

study.oneStory:
The first murder in the Bible is answered by blood crying from the ground, and this chapter is where that cry finally has a hearing in heaven. From Abel onward the story has been one of the righteous killed and the question of when God will make it right. The prophets asked it, the psalmists asked it, and the souls under the altar ask it now, so the fifth seal gathers the whole of that long ache into one scene and puts it before the throne.

The four riders unpack what Genesis 3 set in motion. Sin brought death into the world, Romans 5:12, and the curse brought thorns and pain, Genesis 3:17 to 19. Conquest, bloodshed, scarcity and death are the four faces of that fallen order, and the covenant curses of Leviticus and Ezekiel named them for Israel in particular. The seals say that these are not outside the story of redemption but part of the road through it, and that they are held within the limit of a fourth of the earth and a measured price of wheat.

The sixth seal brings the creation story into reverse. On the fourth day of Genesis 1 God set the sun, moon and stars in the sky, and here they are darkened and thrown down. The order that was called good is shaken, because the creation shares in the fate of the people who rule it. And the fear of the great ones echoes the first fear, the pair hiding among the trees from the sound of the LORD God, Genesis 3:8. The instinct to hide from God is as old as the garden, and here it fills the whole earth.

But the chapter is not the end. The martyrs are given white robes, and the rest of the book will fill that picture out. In chapter 7 a multitude stands in the very robes, in chapter 19 the rider on the white horse is Faithful and True, and in chapter 20 the slain reign. Finally in chapter 21 the old order of death, mourning and pain passes away, Revelation 21:4. The seals show the story at its darkest, but the dark has a limit, a Lord and an end.

sermon.title: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
sermon.why: Carson preaches directly through Revelation 6, working seal by seal from the four horsemen through the martyrs' cry to the sixth seal's cosmic terror, and closes by pointing to the slain Lamb as the only refuge from the very wrath this chapter describes, engaging the full sweep of this section.

quiz.q: Who breaks each of the six seals in this chapter?

options.text: The Lamb, established in chapter 5 as alone worthy to open the scroll.
options.note: Every seal in this chapter is explicitly broken by the Lamb, verses 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 12.

options.text: One of the twenty-four elders, acting on the Lamb's behalf.
options.note: The elders worship throughout Revelation, but it is the Lamb Himself, not an elder, who breaks each seal.

options.text: The four living creatures, who summon the horsemen without the Lamb's involvement.
options.note: The living creatures call out 'Come' after each seal is opened, but it is the Lamb who does the opening.

options.text: An angel sent from the altar of incense.
options.note: The altar and its angel appear later, in chapter 8; the seals in this chapter are broken by the Lamb alone.

quiz.q: What do the second, third, and fourth seals release upon the earth?

options.text: War and bloodshed, severe famine-level scarcity, and death by sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts.
options.note: Verses 3-8 describe exactly these three riders and their effects.

options.text: Only peace and abundance across the whole earth.
options.note: The opposite; peace is taken away and scarcity, not abundance, follows.

options.text: A single plague of locusts covering a third of the earth.
options.note: Locusts appear later, in the fifth trumpet of chapter 9, not among these three seals.

options.text: Total, immediate destruction of the entire earth with no survivors.
options.note: The fourth seal explicitly limits its authority to a fourth of the earth; the judgment is severe but bounded.

quiz.q: What do the martyred souls under the altar cry out for in the fifth seal, and what are they told?

options.text: They cry, 'How long until You judge and avenge our blood,' and are told to rest a little longer until the full number of martyrs is complete.
options.note: Verses 9-11 record this exact cry and the answer given to them.

options.text: They cry for mercy on their persecutors and are granted it immediately.
options.note: Their cry is for justice and vindication, not for mercy on their persecutors, and the answer is to wait, not immediate action.

options.text: They ask to be sent back to earth to finish their mission.
options.note: Their request concerns God's judgment and vindication, not a return to earthly mission.

options.text: They are silenced and told never to speak again.
options.note: They are given white robes and told to rest, not silenced; their cry is heard and answered with a promise.

quiz.q: What happens when the Lamb opens the sixth seal?

options.text: A great earthquake, the sun and moon darkened, stars falling, and every class of person hiding in terror from the wrath of the Lamb.
options.note: Verses 12-17 describe exactly this cosmic upheaval and universal terror.

options.text: A season of complete peace descends on the earth.
options.note: The opposite occurs; the sixth seal brings terrifying cosmic disturbance, not peace.

options.text: Only the wicked kings of the earth are affected, while everyone else remains untouched.
options.note: The text names kings, nobles, commanders, the rich, the mighty, slave, and free, a comprehensive list, not kings alone.

options.text: The scroll is fully opened and history reaches its final end.
options.note: The scroll's full opening awaits the seventh seal in chapter 8; the sixth seal itself brings terror, not the final consummation.

quiz.q: What is the significance of describing the coming judgment as 'the wrath of the Lamb' in verse 16?

options.text: It shows the same Lamb once slain for sinners is also the sovereign judge whose wrath none can withstand.
options.note: This paradox is central to the chapter's climax and to Revelation's larger portrait of Christ.

options.text: It means the wrath belongs only to angels, not to Christ Himself.
options.note: The text specifically names the wrath as belonging to the Lamb and to the One on the throne, not to angels.

options.text: It shows that lambs are naturally fierce and dangerous animals.
options.note: The force of the phrase is theological paradox, sacrificial gentleness paired with righteous judgment, not a comment on animal behavior.

options.text: It indicates the wrath has already ended by this point in the vision.
options.note: The wrath is described as just arriving, 'the great day of their wrath has come,' not as already past.

questions: The four horsemen ride out only because the Lamb permits it. When the news feels like conquest, war, scarcity, and death are winning, how does remembering the Lamb's sovereignty change the way you carry that weight?
The martyrs under the altar were told to wait 'a little while longer.' Where in your own life do you need to trust God's timing for justice rather than demanding it on your own schedule?
Even in famine, the seals held back total destruction, sparing the oil and the wine. Where have you seen God's restraint even in hard seasons, a mercy mixed into judgment?

The sixth seal left every class of person, from kings to slaves, with nowhere to hide except in terror. What would it mean for you to find your hiding place in the Lamb's mercy now, rather than dreading His wrath later?

This chapter has been read by faithful Christians as describing the first century, all of church history, a future tribulation, or the ongoing pattern of this present age. How does holding these different views with humility, while still trusting the chapter's central truth, shape the way you read difficult or uncertain parts of Scripture?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote explains the Greek literally reads 'a choenix of wheat for a denarius,' a choenix being a Greek dry measure of about 1.92 pints, and a denarius customarily a laborer's full day's wage, underscoring just how severe the pictured scarcity is.

The cry 'fall on us and hide us' echoes Hosea 10:8 almost word for word, rooting this scene of terror in an already ancient prophetic warning of judgment on unfaithful Israel, now applied to the whole unrepentant earth.

Some manuscript traditions, including the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus, read 'His wrath' rather than 'Their wrath' in verse 17; the plural reading ties the wrath jointly to both the One on the throne and the Lamb named in verse 16.
